title: How to Break Into Senior Leadership Roles
author: Ethan Evans
summary: Ethan Evans, a former Amazon vice president, lays out a five-step system for moving from strong individual contributor or manager to senior leadership. He opens with the claim that hard work alone does not get people promoted, because executives choose people they like working with and trust. The steps are to find and close gaps by asking the boss what it would take to support a promotion, to deliver a standout result that can be summed up in one short "tweet," to create some worry about losing you without issuing a threat, to treat reorgs as promotion opportunities, and to repeat. He illustrates the tweet idea with his own TiVo integration at Prime Video. He also advises mapping the real decision makers and building relationships before a reorg starts. The post ends with one action for today and a plug for his cohort course.
points: Replace "How am I doing?" with a direct question such as "What would it take for you to support my promotion in the next cycle?", and warn the boss in advance.
Promotion cases depend on a short, memorable reason, a tweet like "Without Ethan, we wouldn't have had TiVo," not a long list of accomplishments.
Signal ambition without an ultimatum, for example by saying your career matters to you and you need to know whether it matters to the company.
Reorgs can move faster than promotion cycles, so tell your boss ahead of time you want more scope and build ties with whoever will decide.
Each promotion resets the job, so the cycle of feedback, gap closing, and a new standout result starts again.
quotes: I need this because executives do not have time to initially process a giant document explaining everything you have accomplished.
Instead, ask a question that forces an answer: “What would it take for you to support my promotion in the next cycle?
Hitting every target and reliably doing your job is good, but it is not enough.
If you don’t promote me, I’ll quit” is an ultimatum that can make you seem uncooperative and may cause your boss to start planning for your departure, which means even less of a chance at promotion.
Reorgs can move faster than promotion cycles, and there is not necessarily a formal packet and panel needed for you to move up.
You can be brilliant, but if I do not like spending time with you or trust how you make decisions, promoting you creates a new problem for me.
Every time you move up, the job changes. Suddenly you are inexperienced again. You have new weaknesses.
